slides.title: What is Natural Language Processing (NLP)
slides.text:
What is Natural Language Processing (NLP)
•  NLP is a subfield of AI that enables computers & robots to understand, interpret
   and generate human language.
                                                         Response
                                                            Generation
                                              Speech
                                                 Recognition

                                             Language
                                             Understanding

 Human-human interaction       Human-robot interaction
•  Methodology: by developing a model that can analyse the
   linguistic structure, meaning and context in both written
   (input as text) and spoken (input as speech) forms.

slides.title: Why NLP matters in Robotics
slides.text:
Why NLP matters in Robotics

•  NLP helps robots understand human instructions.                                                                    •   Applications in Robotics
•  Modern AI can help robots:                                              – Human-Robot Interaction
    –  understand spoken or written commands                 (HRI)
    –  identify objects and locations                   –  Voice-Controlled Robots
    –  plan sequences of actions                      –  Navigation
    –  interact naturally with humans                  –  Task Planning & Execution
•  Example command: “Pick up the red ball near the chair!”
•  An efficient NLP system must extract
    −  the action (pick up)
    −  the object (ball)
    −  the object properties (red)
    −  the object location (near chair)
•  The robot then plans and executes the task.

                                                                                                           5

visualInspection.notes: Command Pick up the red ball near the chair decomposed into action pick up, target ball, attribute red and spatial relation near chair. Right list HRI/voice/navigation/planning. Planning and execution follow extraction, not identical to token recognition.

slides.title: Challenges of Human Language
slides.text:
Challenges of Human Language
•  The main challenges (with example commands) that prevent a robot from
   learning human commands are:
    –  Ambiguity: the same word with more than one meaning
           •  “Pick up the light box” – does light mean lightweight or illuminated?
    –  Accents: the same word can be pronounced differently by people from different places
           •  “Fetch the ball” – The robot may mishear bowl for ball
    – Synonyms: Words with similar meanings
           • Humans may say: “fetch”, ”pick”, or “take” the object
           – Can robots understand that?
    –  Context: AI models struggle to detect sarcasm/tone/body
       language
           •  “Great job, robot!” from humans may be genuine
             praise or frustration after failure.

                                                                                                           6

visualInspection.notes: Four challenge examples actually viewed: light lightweight/illuminated ambiguity; ball/bowl accent-related misrecognition; fetch/pick/take contextual synonyms; Great job genuine praise or frustration. Both senses of light shown here can be adjectives, unlike later POS noun/adjective example; do not conflate the two.

slides.title: NLP Pipeline
slides.text:
NLP Pipeline
•  These stages are conceptual.
•   In modern NLP systems, multiple stages may happen together internally.



•  The Pre-processing step includes:
    –  Step 1: Convert text to lowercase
    –  Step 2: Remove punctuations
    –  Step 3: Tokenization
    –  Step 4: Remove stopwords
    –  Step 5: Stemming or Lemmatization

• We use nltk (Natural Language Toolkit) Python library for general NLP tasks.

                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: Diagram sequence is Human Speech/Text → Pre-Processing → Numerical Representation/Vectorization → Language Understanding → Robot Planning → Robot Action. The text explicitly calls stages conceptual and allows joint internal processing. Listed preprocessing order lowercasing, punctuation removal, tokenization, stopwords, stemming/lemmatization. NLTK full name shown.

slides.title: Pre-processing - Tokenization
slides.text:
Pre-processing - Tokenization
 •   It is the process by which machines learn language by breaking sentences into
    smaller units called tokens.
 •   All the extracted tokens are stored in a list.
 •  For an input: “Pick up the red ball near the chair”        Vocabulary ≡ Dictionary
                                                              Corpus ≡ Library
    – The entire collection of unique words/tokens
      known to the NLP system is known as vocabulary.
             •  E.g. pick, up, the, red, ball, near, the, chair
             • The system matches words in the given command to
          known tokens in its vocabulary.
    – A corpus is a large collection of text like books,
        websites, etc used to train NLP systems, to build
        vocabulary.


                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: Tokenization and list displayed. Vocabulary explicitly unique, but the indented example repeats the; it is an eight-token sequence with seven unique types. Corpus is collection of texts used for training/vocabulary. Dictionary/library analogy is mnemonic, not a storage-type specification. Tokenization alone does not mean the machine has learned semantics.

slides.title: Pre-processing - Stop Words, Stemming & Lemmatization
slides.text:
Pre-processing - Stop Words, Stemming & Lemmatization
•  Stop words: Common words that carry little meaning and are often removed
   during processing. Example: is, a, the, etc.
•  Stemming: Reducing words to their root/base form.
    –  Example: playing, played, plays → play
•  Stemming removes word endings mechanically, while lemmatization converts
   words into meaningful base forms.

        Word           Stemming        Lemmatization

         studies               studi               study
•  Removing stop words, followed by lemmatization help robots:
    −process commands faster
    −recognize actions more easily
   −reduce language complexity


                                                                                                           9

visualInspection.notes: Stopwords is/a/the, stemming plays/played/playing→play, table studies→studi versus study. Claims faster processing/easier action recognition/lower complexity are task-dependent; removing words can remove relevant relations or negation. Stemming may give nonword; lemma meaningful base.

slides.title: Vectorization: Representing Language Numerically
slides.text:
Vectorization: Representing Language Numerically
•  Humans understand meaning, emotion and context from language clearly.
•  But, computers can only process numbers (math operations, vectors, etc)
•   Just like images become pixel values, language (unstructured) must become
   numbers (structured data).
•  Hence, the core idea is to turn words into vectors.
•  There are several techniques to convert text to vectors.
•  They are:
    – One-Hot Encoding
    – Bag of Words (BOW)
    – Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF)
    – Word Embeddings like Word2Vec & GloVe



                                                                                                          12

visualInspection.notes: Vectorization motivation, pixel analogy, and four methods one-hot/BoW/TF-IDF/Word2Vec-GloVe viewed. Humans understand context clearly is pedagogical contrast, not guarantee all humans resolve ambiguity. Numerical encoding is necessary for computation but not equivalent to semantic correctness.

slides.title: One-hot encoding & Bag of Words
slides.text:
One-hot encoding & Bag of Words
1.  One-Hot Encoding: is the most common method. Every word in your dictionary
    (vocabulary) will be represented as a binary vector
      •  Each token will be a unique combination of 0s and 1s.
      •  Limitations:
        ꟷcreates very large, sparse matrices
        ꟷDoesn’t capture the relationship between other words
2.  Bag of Words (BoW): represents a command by counting how many times each
   word from the vocabulary appears.
      •   It creates a vector for an entire command, unlike One-Hot
       Encoding, which represents a single word
      •  Limitations:
        ꟷIgnores word order and context
        ꟷSparsity


                                                                                                          13

visualInspection.notes: One-hot and BoW conceptual descriptions actually viewed. Token-level one-hot distinguishes identity, command-level unigram counts discard order/context. Both sparse and high-dimensional; most common is a temporal generalization, not a timeless fact. Count representation is not restricted to binary values.

slides.title: TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency)
slides.text:
TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency)

3.  TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency):
      •  TF-IDF measures:
      ꟷhow often a word appears in a command
      ꟷhow important or unique that word is across many commands/documents
      •  Term Frequency (TF): Measures how often a word appears in the current
      command/document.
                      𝐍𝐨. 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝒕 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝒅
           𝐓𝐅𝒕, 𝒅=
                          𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐧𝐨. 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝒅
      •  Note: here, term & document mean token & a
        single/collection of commands, respectively.
      •  Unlike BoW, TF-IDF does not simply count words. It gives:
       ꟷlower importance to very common words
       ꟷhigher importance to informative/rare words


                                                                                                          16

visualInspection.notes: Normalized term-frequency fraction viewed: term count divided by total terms in document. Documents may be single command or explicitly grouped commands; numerical work must fix boundaries and tokenization. Rarer terms are emphasized only relative to TF and corpus.

slides.title: TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency)
slides.text:
TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency)

•   Inverse Document Frequency (IDF): Measures how unique or rare a word is across the
    entire dataset (the corpus 𝐷).
•  Common words get lower importance.
•  Rare words get higher importance.
                                    𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐧𝐨. 𝐨𝐟 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝑵
              𝐈𝐃𝐅𝒕, 𝑫= 𝒍𝒐𝒈(                               𝐍𝐨. 𝐨𝐟 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝒕 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦)

               𝐓𝐅−𝐈𝐃𝐅𝒕, 𝒅, 𝐃= 𝐓𝐅𝒕, 𝒅 × 𝐈𝐃𝐅(𝒕, 𝑫)

    Note:
     •  A corpus will have many documents
     •  A document will have many terms/tokens.
     •  Hence, BoW and TF-IDF use word tokens to generate vector
       representations of entire documents or commands.



                                                                                                          17

visualInspection.notes: IDF=log(total documents/documents containing term), followed by TF-IDF product, actually viewed. Log base unspecified. Document frequency counts presence, not repeated occurrences; zero document frequency makes unsmoothed formula undefined. Ubiquitous terms have zero IDF under this formula.

Word Embeddings
4.  Word Embeddings (Word2Vec & GloVe)

        vectorization, where words are

       continuous space.
    – Word2Vec or GloVe use neural networks
        to learn vectors & uses Cosine Similarity
        to place words with similar meaning
        closer to each other.

slides.title: Language Understanding
slides.text:
Language Understanding
 •  After converting text into numerical representations (vectors), NLP models
    begin extracting meaning from the command.
 •  Two important language understanding tasks are:
    –  Parts of Speech (POS) Tagging
    – Named Entity Recognition (NER)
 •  Modern NLP systems internally use vectorized representations of words/tokens
    to perform tasks like POS tagging and NER.
 •  Although we conceptually separate vectorization & language understanding,
  many modern AI systems perform these operations
   together internally.
 •  Traditional NLP systems often used POS tagging before
   NER, while modern transformer-based systems can learn
   both tasks together.

                                                                                                          20

visualInspection.notes: Language understanding slide viewed; POS and NER named; explicit conceptual separation of vectorization versus meaning extraction, often performed together. Traditional POS-before-NER example versus joint modern modeling does not mandate all architectures.

slides.title: Core NLP Tasks and their Application in Robotics
slides.text:
Core NLP Tasks and their Application in Robotics

 1. Text Classification: process of assigning a predefined category to an entire
 piece of text such as a command.
       •  In Robotics, it can be seen as Intent Classification
       •  For fields like HRI, knowing the intention of the human is unavoidable.
       •  A robot doesn't just need to know the words; it needs to classify the Intent of
        the human.
       •   It allows the robot to trigger the correct action.
       •  Examples:
             •  Input: "Can you find the charger?" → Class: Navigation
             •  Input: "Stop immediately!" → Class: Emergency
             •  Input: "Lift the small crate." → Class: Manipulation




                                                                                                          24

visualInspection.notes: Text classification assigns predefined category to entire text; robotics intent classification triggers task class. Examples charger→Navigation, stop immediately→Emergency, lift small crate→Manipulation are task taxonomy, not universal unique labels.

slides.title: Core NLP Tasks and their Application in Robotics
slides.text:
Core NLP Tasks and their Application in Robotics

 2. Sentiment Analysis: Detects the emotion or tone behind the words.
       •  Essential for Service Robots or Social Robots.
        ꟷIf a human says "Great job, robot!" with frustration after a failure, the
            robot needs to detect the Negative Sentiment (sarcasm) rather than just
            the literal words.
 3. Machine Translation: Translates text from one language to another.
       •  Multilingual robot can function in places like airports, where people from all
        over the world will be present.
 4.  Question Answering: Extracting an answer from a
    knowledge base.
       •  Robots acts as a mobile interface/assistant for information




                                                                                                          25

visualInspection.notes: All three task definitions and application examples viewed: sentiment with sarcastic Great job after failure; machine translation for multilingual airports; question answering from a knowledge base with robot mobile interface. Not all QA must be extractive; source example is explicitly knowledge-base answering.

slides.title: Core NLP Tasks and their Application in Robotics
slides.text:
Core NLP Tasks and their Application in Robotics
 5. Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR)
       •  Converts Speech into Text. This process is called transcription.
       •  This is how mostly robots receive commands for processing in HRI
       •  A complete HRI pipeline using ASR would look like:



       •  The NLP processing stage may include preprocessing, vectorization, intent detection,
        language understanding & contextual understanding
       •  ASR itself do not understand language
       •  Commonly used STT model: OpenAI whisper model
       •  ASR is used in voice-controlled robots, smart assistants
      home automation, healthcare robots, humanoid robots, etc


                                                                                                          26

visualInspection.notes: All ASR bullets and five-box diagram viewed. Human speech→ASR speech-to-text→NLP extraction→robot planning→execution. NLP includes preprocessing/vectorization/intent/context. Whisper listed as STT example. ASR task output is a transcript, not by itself a grounded executable plan; source claim no language understanding is task-level simplification, not proof models use no context.

slides.title: Problems with traditional NLP systems
slides.text:
Problems with traditional NLP systems
•   Traditional NLP systems:
    –  processed words one-by-one      −  often forgot the earlier context
    –  struggled with long sentences
•  This created difficulties in robotics tasks involving:
    –  long instructions                     −pronouns and references
    –  multiple objects    −complex task planning
•   It struggles with commands like: “Move the robot toward the shelf because it is
   cluttered”
•  The struggle: What does it refer to?
•  The robot must understand:
      •  object relationships
      •  context                       •  instruction sequence
•  Solution: Transformers

                                                                                                          27

visualInspection.notes: Traditional NLP limitations and cluttered-shelf pronoun example viewed. Listed long instructions, multiple objects, pronouns/references and complex planning. Broad word-by-word and forgetting characterizations must be bounded to systems with limited contextual modeling, not every historical model.

slides.title: Transformers
slides.text:
Transformers
•  Transformers revolutionised NLP by enabling models to understand words based
   on their surrounding context rather than processing them independently.
•  Example commands:
    –  C1: Move the robot toward the shelf because it is cluttered.          Note what
                                                                                                             it refers to
                                                                                        in each
                                                            command.
    −  C2: Move the robot toward the shelf because it is low on battery.



•   Transformers use attention mecahnism to analyze relationships
   between words using surrounding context, which is
   demonstrated by the boldness of the arrows.

                                                                                                          28

visualInspection.notes: Both attention diagrams actually viewed. Bold strongest schematic arrow links shelf to it in cluttered sentence, robot to it in low-battery sentence. Pale arrows do not provide numerical normalized weights. Text describes surrounding context and attention; common-sense referents are intended examples, not guaranteed inference for every possible world.

slides.title: Transformers
slides.text:
Transformers
•  Using attention mechanism, transformers can learn:
    – Which words are important
    – Which words are related
    – Where the model should focus
•   In the command C1, the robot must focus on:
    – “move” : the action
    –  “robot” : object to be moved
    –  “shelf” : spatial context
•  This helps the model to connect related words, track
   context and understand references and relationships
• When transformer models were trained on massive
  amounts of text and scaled to billions of parameters, they
   evolved into Large Language Models (LLMs).

                                                                                                          29

visualInspection.notes: Attention can learn importance/relations/focus; C1 slots move action, robot moved object, shelf spatial context. Linking words tracks references and relations. Text-data and parameter scaling described as path to LLMs; not a necessary-and-sufficient threshold definition.

slides.title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
slides.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs)
•  LLMs are AI systems trained on massive amounts of text data to:
     1.  understand language             3. summarize information    5. answer questions
     2.  generate human-like responses  4. follow instructions
•  Examples: ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama
•  They’re built using Transformer architectures. They process text by:
                                                       3. generating responses token-by-token     1.  analyzing context
     2.  predicting the next token (word/subword)


                                      Note: 𝐩𝐰𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐱𝐭
                                           gives the probability
                                          of the next word w.r.t
                                                 context.



                                                                                                          30

visualInspection.notes: Entire LLM slide and probability table viewed. Definition/tasks/examples, transformer architecture and context→next-token→token-by-token generation. Diagram input pick, candidate up .57, and .35, your .15, it .07 with ellipsis; these four labeled probabilities already sum to 1.14, impossible for mutually exclusive next-token distribution. Preserve as-printed ranking, distinguish explicitly renormalized supplied weight exercise; ellipsis cannot fix excess mass.

slides.title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
slides.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs)
•  By learning to predict the next word across billions of sentences, LLMs learn
   grammar, context, relationship between words & reasoning patterns.
•  This will enable LLMs to help robots with:
    –  understand flexible commands −plan multi-step tasks −ask clarification questions
    –  interact conversationally      −explain their actions



•  But LLMs don’t truly understand human language. They:
      •  hallucinate (generate incorrect information)
      •  misunderstand instructions
•  In robotics, incorrect understanding can lead to unsafe
   actions.


                                                                                                          31

visualInspection.notes: All LLM capability/risk bullets and four-box diagram viewed. Flexible commands, conversation, multi-step plans, explanations and clarification. Human command→LLM→robot planning→robot action. Hallucinated information and misunderstood instructions can create unsafe physical actions. Do not turn contested truly understand phrase into objective consciousness claim.

slides.title: Beyond LLMs: Multimodal AI in Robotics
slides.text:
Beyond LLMs: Multimodal AI in Robotics
•  Modern robots increasingly combine LLMs with
   vision, sensors, and planning systems to achieve
  more natural human-robot interaction.
1.  Vision Language Models(VLMs): input becomes
    a combination of image & text
    –  It has an additional vision backbone called Vision
       Transformer (ViT), which is a transformer
        architecture modified to process images.
    – The visual tokens from the ViT are mapped into the
       LLM, allowing the LLM to see the image patches as
            if they were just part of the text prompt.
    –  Examples: DeepSeek-VL2, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-
        4o, Llama 3.2, NVLM, Qwen 2.5-VL


                                                                                                          32

visualInspection.notes: VLM image+text diagram and all bullets viewed. Illustrated ViT produces mapped visual tokens for language processing; not every VLM must have this exact backbone. Mug image plus red-object question; labels mug .78,cup .15,desk .04,pencil .02 with ellipsis (sum .99, possible .01 omitted mass). Listed model names are source examples not current benchmark/ranking.

slides.title: Beyond LLMs: Multimodal AI in Robotics
slides.text:
Beyond LLMs: Multimodal AI in Robotics
2. Vision Language Action (VLA) Models extend VLMs by adding robot actions.
   ꟷThey connect vision, language & physical
       robot control
   ꟷTo make actions compatible with transformer
        architectures, VLAs often tokenize continuous
        robotic actions (like joint angles or end-
        effector positions) into discrete values, treating
       a physical movement exactly like a word in a
       vocabulary sentence.
   ꟷVLAs enable robots to understand language,
       detect objects, plan movement & execute
        actions.
    ꟷExamples: RT-2 (Robotics Transformer 2) by
       Google DeepMind, OpenVLA

                                                                                                          33

visualInspection.notes: VLA diagram and text actually viewed. Mug image and pick up instruction; VLM Encoder and Action Prediction Head inside VLA; next embodied state after execution and visual update. Joint angles/end-effector positions discretized in many designs, not universal necessity; movement like a word is representation analogy, not equivalence of safety/semantics. Figure object-label probabilities .65,.10,.04,.02 with ellipses are not calibrated joint coordinates. Examples RT-2 and OpenVLA.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary
•  NLP is essential for computers/robots to understand human language.
•  The NLP pipeline includes pre-processing, tokenization, language understanding,
   vectorization and decision making
•  These techniques help convert human language into machine-understandable
   representations.
•  But they severely lack an understanding of context.
•  Transformers introduced contextual understanding, attention mechanisms and
   improved handling of long instructions and references
•  Modern LLMs were built using transformers.
•  Modern robotics increasingly combines language, vision,
   sensors, planning & robotic control, bringing multimodality
•  VLMs & VLAs are such resulting architectures.


                                                                                                           34

visualInspection.notes: All summary bullets viewed and compared. Listed pipeline components not explicitly ordered and must not override earlier arrow diagram. Context and transformer broad claims repeat prior simplifications. No new code, equation, worked example or unique concept.
